children: Palo Alto Networks Chief Executive Nikesh Arora may have confused some investors when he coined the term "platformization" a few years ago to describe a trend toward consolidated solutions in the cybersecurity industry.
Now, the word itself remains a mouthful, but the underlying thesis is as clear as ever.

The cybersecurity company reported around 220 net platformizations in the fiscal fourth quarter, its term to describe upgrading customers to an integrated cybersecurity platform. That's about double its total from the previous quarter, and evidence that artificial intelligence is driving demand for holistic cyber solutions, Arora said in an interview.

"The enterprise customers are beginning to realize that they have so much to deal with that they are basically defaulting to trusted partners in the cybersecurity space who they believe will be there for the duration and will be their partners for the long term," Arora said. "We're seeing that play out in spades."

By fiscal year 2030, the company is aiming to complete at least 4,000 platformizations supporting its target of $20 billion in Next-Generation Security annual recurring revenue. The uptick in platformized customers, who the company says deliver upwards of 120% net revenue retention, gives Palo Alto more confidence in its targets.

"It just reinforces to us that that was the right strategy," Arora said. "The accelerating pace of platformization will allow us to get there and gives us more comfort to get there. It tells us the customers are beginning to see the value in the strategy that we've articulated."

Palo Alto's focus on platforms dovetails with an aggressive mergers-and-acquisitions strategy, with big-ticket acquisitions of CyberArk and Chronosphere followed up by more recent deals to buy agentic AI company Console and observability platform Embrace.

Though some investors have raised questions about the balance of Palo Alto's organic and inorganic growth, Arora said Palo Alto's leadership propelled both CyberArk and Chronosphere to their best-ever quarters. The company can "turbocharge" its acquired assets through scaling, innovation, and go-to-market capabilities, he said.

The consolidation craze is also extending to Palo Alto's competitors. CrowdStrike's finance chief last week said 51% of its customers had adopted at least six modules and that 26% have at least eight, crediting the "power of our platform strategy" with driving 26% revenue growth in its second quarter.

For Palo Alto, platformizations helped propel its company's Next-Generation Security ARR up 63% to $9.1 billion, with revenue up 34% to $3.41 billion in the fourth quarter. Shares were down 10% to $325.94 in Wednesday's session.

Arora said that as new vulnerabilities from AI drive innovation in the industry, it's only natural that consolidation follows shortly behind. He likened it to consolidation that has taken place over time in markets for enterprise resource planning and customer-relationship-management software, saying cybersecurity is following a similar trajectory.

"The winners were the ones who actually built integrated platforms and sold them over those 20 years, not the ones who tried to keep them separate and keep them fragmented," Arora said of the ERP and CRM markets. "There's no reason why it should not continue to happen in cybersecurity."
